body.p: Claims 11, 29, and 30 are Currently Amended. Claims 1-10 were previously canceled. Claims 11-30 are currently pending.
Claims 11 and 29 are amended to overcome potential antecedent basis rejections. Applicant respectfully requests withdrawal of the rejections.
Claims 11, 13-23, and 25-30 are rejected as being unpatentable over Chahine et al. (US 2017/0056644) in view of Jain et al. (US 2016/0287128). Claims 11 and 29 have been amended.
1. Jain does not teach "at least one textile-based ECG generator electrode for
transmitting a generated signal through the user's skin," as recited by amended claims

As an initial matter, the Office Action, at page 5, states, when referring to the disclosure of Jain, that "[t]he Examiner considers electrodes that are integrated into clothing [in Jain] as being 'textile-based' electrodes." Applicant respectfully disagrees. The Office Action, moreover, states that Chahine does not explicitly disclose textile-based electrodes that are "ECG" electrodes, and turns to Jain. Jain, however, does not teach or suggest textile-based ECG generator electrodes as claimed.

Claim 11 has been amended to clarify "at least one textile-based ECG generator electrode for transmitting a generated signal through the user's skin," and a controller device configured to transmit "a generated signal through the at least one textile-based ECG generator electrode, and sense a collected signal from the at least one textile-based ECG generator electrode via the one or more textile-based ECG receiver electrode." These features, among other features of amended claim 11, are not shown to be disclosed or suggested by the asserted prior art.
For example, contrary to the assertion in the Office Action, the "right leg drive (RLD) generator 14" of Jain is not "at least one textile-based ECG generator electrode" as recited in
amended claim 11. Jain describes a "sensor pad 7" that has "contactless ECG sensors" and "also ... a right leg drive (RLD) generator 14":
which may be provided in ch as that shown in FIG. 2. The sensor pad 7 may also include a grounding pad 15, a driving circuitry e.g. a right leg
drive (RLD) generator 14 (discussed below), and an ND converter 13.

Jain, para [0087] (emphasis added). Fig. 8 of Jain (reproduced below) similarly shows that the "right leg drive generator 14" is not a "contactless ECG sensors 10" and as such is not "at least one textile-based ECG generator electrode" as recited in amended claim 11. Accordingly, Applicant submits that Jain does not teach or suggest among other features of amended claim 11, "at least one textile-based ECG generator electrode for transmitting a generated signal." and a controller device configured to transmit "a generated signal through the at least one textile-based ECG generator electrode, and sense a collected signal from the at least one textile-based ECG generator electrode via the one or more textile-based ECG receiver electrode."
2. One of skill in the art would not combine a textile electrode with a contactless
electrode.

The Office Action, and the references, provides no motivation or suggestion for why a person of skill in the art would combine a non-ECG textile electrode, as alleged by the Office Action is taught by Chahine, with a contactless ECG electrode as alleged by the Office Action is taught by Jain. Applicant submits that the only motivation comes from a hindsight bias. Therefore, Applicant submits that the rejection is predicated on impermissible hindsight bias.
Furthermore, a proper obviousness combination requires a reasonable expectation of

success, as described in MPEP § 2143.02. The Office Action provides no teaching or description as to how one skilled in the art could reasonably expect to modify the contactless ECG sensors disclosed in Jain to arrive at an operable textile-based ECG electrode as in the claims 11 and 29.
3. Jain fails to teach or suggest that "the controller detects whether one or more of the
plurality of textile-based ECG electrodes are in acceptable contact with the skin of the
user," as recited by claim 13.
The Office Action asserts that paragraph [0039] of Jain describes the controller detects

whether one or more of the plurality of textile-based ECG electrodes are in acceptable contact with the skin of the user. However, as described above, Jain describes contactless ECG sensors and not "textile-based ECG electrodes comprising interlaced conductive fibers for conducting a plurality of ECG signals with respect to the upper body of the user while in contact with skin of the user." Thus, the controller is not configured to detect whether the plurality of textile-based ECG electrodes are in acceptable contact with the skin of the user.
At least for this reason, claim 13 is considered to be patentable over the cited art.
